nameStory: The 'horned' grebe gets its name from the striking golden-orange feather tufts that stick out like little horns above and behind its eyes during breeding season. These aren't actually horns at all, but rather decorative plumes that make this small waterbird look like it's wearing a fancy feathered crown!
description: The Horned Grebe is a compact, duck-like waterbird that's smaller than most ducks you'll see on New England waters. During breeding season, it sports a dramatic black head with bright golden-orange 'horns' and a rusty-red neck, but in winter it transforms into a much plainer black-and-white bird. Like all grebes, it has lobed toes instead of webbed feet and sits low in the water with its pointed bill ready to spear small fish. You'll most often spot these diving birds on lakes, ponds, and coastal waters where they disappear underwater for several seconds at a time while hunting.

idTips.label: Golden horns
idTips.description: In breeding plumage, look for the distinctive bright golden-orange feather tufts that flare out behind the eyes like tiny horns - no other small waterbird has this feature

idTips.label: Diving behavior
idTips.description: Watch for the characteristic grebe dive - they slip underwater smoothly without the splashing jump of a duck, often staying under for 10-30 seconds

idTips.label: Winter plumage
idTips.description: In fall and winter, becomes a clean black-and-white bird with dark cap extending below the eye and bright white cheeks and neck

idTips.label: Bill shape
idTips.description: Straight, pointed bill that looks like a tiny dagger - perfect for spearing small fish and aquatic insects

idTips.label: Water position
idTips.description: Sits very low in the water with just head, neck, and a bit of back visible - much lower profile than most ducks

idTips.label: Size reference
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller and more compact than a Mallard, with a rounder body and shorter neck than other diving birds

habitat: In New England, Horned Grebes are found on open freshwater lakes, large ponds, and coastal bays, especially during migration and winter. They prefer waters deep enough for diving, often gathering in small flocks on larger lakes like Lake Champlain or along the coast in protected harbors and estuaries. During winter, they're commonly seen in saltwater environments including coastal ponds and quiet bays.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration occurs in April and May when birds pass through in breeding plumage, showing off those spectacular golden horns and rusty necks. Look for them on larger lakes and coastal waters during this brief but spectacular window.
seasonality.summer: Most Horned Grebes continue north to breed in Canada, so summer sightings in New England are uncommon. Any summer birds are likely non-breeding individuals or rare local nesters on remote northern lakes.
seasonality.fall: Fall migration brings them back in September and October, now molting into winter plumage. Birds may show a mixed appearance with some breeding feathers still visible alongside emerging winter colors.
seasonality.winter: Winter residents arrive in full black-and-white plumage, often staying on unfrozen coastal waters and large inland lakes. They're most reliably found during this season, often in small flocks.

funFact: Horned Grebes have one of the most dramatic seasonal makeovers in the bird world - the same individual that sports flamboyant golden horns and rusty plumage in spring becomes so plain in winter that many birdwatchers don't recognize it as the same species!
confusionNotes: Winter Horned Grebes are easily confused with Pied-billed Grebes, but remember 'dark cap dips' - the Horned Grebe's black cap extends down below the eye level, while the Pied-billed Grebe has a lighter face overall and lacks the clean black-and-white contrast.
contextualKnowledge: In Europe, this same species is called the 'Slavonian Grebe,' named after an old region in northern Prussia where they were commonly found. The two names reflect the bird's wide distribution across northern continents, with slightly different subspecies on each side of the Atlantic.
compareHints: Horned Grebes are much smaller and more compact than Red-necked Grebes, which have longer, more snake-like necks and larger bills. The extremely rare Eared Grebe has a more fan-shaped golden crest and appears more 'fluffy' around the head, while Horned Grebes have those distinctive straight horn-like tufts projecting backward from the eyes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red-necked Grebes are significantly larger than their closest New England relatives, the Horned and Eared Grebes.

Compared to its closest New England relatives, Eared Grebes are smaller than Red-necked Grebes (which have rusty necks in breeding plumage) and distinguished from Horned Grebes by their upswept golden ear tufts versus the Horned Grebe's straight-out yellow 'horns.
